item.title: Jensen Huang: Why a personal scandal for the face of the AI boom has provoked a national security scare
item.description: Once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech", Huang is mired in scandal after an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
item.content:encoded:
Jensen Huang is one of the technology industry's most high-profile figures.

He rose to prominence as the business he leads - artificial intelligence (AI) chip giant Nvidia - became one of the world's most valuable companies.

As the face of the AI boom, Huang also became close to Donald Trump as the president pushed for the US to keep its dominance of the technology over China.

The 63-year-old who was once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech" and referred to as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan is now mired in scandal after an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

Who is Jensen Huang?

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US.

He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia.

He has an estimated fortune of $155bn, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine - a biography on Huang, tells the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.

Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang.

Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged.

"I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country".

Huang has long found himself at the centre of US-China tensions. Trump has repeatedly said the two nations are in a race for dominance.

Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.

The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.

Since 2022 the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.

But it means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Jensen Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero. In recent years Huang has engaged in a flurry of shuttle diplomacy, dashing between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.

Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China.

Quarter after quarter of late, Nvidia has been locked out of that lucrative market. Despite his ostensible closeness to Trump, Huang has not managed to wrest this concession from the administration.

What is Nvidia?

Huang founded Nvidia with fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993.

The company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.

Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates.

"In 2012 these machine learning neural net researchers started to use it for that purpose and Jensen immediately recongnised that this was going to be a massive industry and the future of computing. He began to pour enormous amounts of resources into building what was essentially the AI hardware market," says Witt.

"Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them."

Nvidia is now worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever.

"The first real neural net of modern times on an Nvidia network was Alex Krizhevsky's Alexnet and they trained that on two Nvidia cards in Alex's bedroom. Now we do the same thing but we do it with 200,000 - 300,000 cards and instead of doing it in a bedroom we do it in a giant barn full of computers called a data centre," adds Witt.

"So when you think about a data centre buildout, when you hear the AI infrastructure buildout, Jensen runs a tollbooth. All of that goes through him. And it made his company at least temporarily, the most valuable company in the world."

Nvidia's board has announced a probe following reports by the New York Times that Huang had engaged in a romantic relationship with a woman believed by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy.

For now, though, Nvidia's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team".

Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake. There is also no clear successor to the 63-year old tech boss.

Who is Huang's wife?

Huang met his wife Lori at Oregon State University, where she was also studying electrical engineering and was his lab partner.

They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer.

He has credited Lori and Madison for making black leather jackets his signature style.

In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation.

The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.

Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.

"Jensen in my conversations with him and in other conversations has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man. That's very important to him," says Witt.

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways. Both of his children work for Nvidia. Spencer and Maddison. The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."

Huang for his part released a statement which said, "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

What do we know about the affair?

US officials had concluded that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reports.

She was a top executive at Megaspeed, a data centre company based in Singapore. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked.

Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".

It remains unclear what information Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.

Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.

When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not.

"We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC.

Additional reporting by Ayeshea Perera in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney

item.title: Woman says Al Fayed's brother drugged and sexually abused her at Highland estate
item.description: The woman says she was flown to the Fayed family's Balnagown estate, where she was repeatedly assaulted.
item.content:encoded:
A woman has told BBC Scotland how she was trafficked to the Highlands, drugged, sexually assaulted and held prisoner by Salah Fayed, the brother of former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed.

Jill, whose name has been changed for legal reasons, said she was a young Harrods employee when she was recruited to what she believed was an executive training scheme in the 1990s.

Speaking for the first time about the abuse that took place in Scotland, Jill said she was flown on the Fayed family's private jet to Balnagown, their estate in Easter Ross, where she was repeatedly assaulted.

She is one of hundreds of women who have alleged abuse by the Fayed brothers.

Since Mohamed Al Fayed's death in 2023, hundreds of women and girls have alleged they were sexually abused by him.

His brother Salah, who died of pancreatic cancer in 2010, has also been accused of abuse by numerous women.

Police Scotland said three people had been identified in connection with offending against a number of victims at Balnagown and inquiries remained ongoing.

Speaking to BBC Scotland, Jill described Salah Fayed as "a very cruel man" who exploited her vulnerabilities and exercised near-total control over her life.

She said she began her career at Harrods working for Mohamed Al Fayed in a heavily-monitored office staffed largely by young women, where access was tightly controlled and employees were discouraged from interacting with others.

Soon afterwards, she was assigned to work for Salah Fayed.

"I thought it might be better," she said. "Mohamed seemed creepy to me."

Instead, she said, her situation deteriorated rapidly.

"I was taken to Scotland twice. Both times it was on their private jet.

"When you flew there, you flew into Inverness and their vehicles would pick you up from the airport and take you to the estate."

On the Balnagown Estate there were three residences, one for each brother.

Jill describes Salah Fayed's house as smaller than Mohamed Al Fayed's, overlooking the valley with the forest behind and isolated.

She alleged that by this stage Salah Fayed had begun giving her illegal substances.

"The first time he forced me to take the drugs he tried to trick me into taking them," she said.

"He had me locked in a room. He said 'you need to take this, it's good for you'. He lied about what it was and when I refused he screamed at me and forced me to take it.

"The drugs were part of his method of assaulting me."

Jill said he controlled what she ate, wore and who she spoke to.

She said most of what happened was against her will.

"I was isolated, for most of the time," she said. "He was a very cruel man.

"He knew I had some vulnerabilities and he exploited them. He made me feel I was a terrible person."

Jill said escaping the situation was difficult and that she only gradually came to understand the extent of what had happened to her.

"By the time I got away, I was very aware of what he was doing and it took some effort to get away," she said.

"I was by then aware that I could not have been the only one.

"I tried to raise the alarm, I tried to warn people."

Salah Fayed was one of three Fayed brothers who purchased Harrods, the luxury Knightsbridge department store, in 1985.

  • If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support is available at BBC Action Line.

After his death, Mohamed Al Fayed was accused by more than 20 women of sexual assault in a BBC documentary Predator at Harrods that aired in 2024.

Since those allegations more than 400 alleged victims or witnesses have come forward to lawyers.

Earlier this year, Police Scotland said it was carrying out further investigations into allegations connected to Balnagown Estate.

In a statement, a police spokesperson said: "Three people have been identified in connection with offending against a number of victims.

"Our inquiries are ongoing and it would be inappropriate to comment further."

Human trafficking

The Metropolitan Police is separately investigating allegations linked to Mohamed Al Fayed and those suspected of facilitating his offending.

It said it was one of the largest and most complex investigations it was currently undertaking.

"Seven suspects have so far been interviewed under caution on suspicion of offences including aiding and abetting rape and sexual assault, assisting the commission of sexual offences, and human trafficking for sexual exploitation," a Met Police statement said.

"To date, 168 victims have now come forward. We will continue to assess victim testimonies for evidence of human trafficking."

In a confidential note, shared with survivors, of a meeting between the Met and the All Party Parliamentary Group for Survivors of Fayed and Harrods, it said about 70 people had been referred to the Home Office as potential victims of trafficking.

Jill told BBC Scotland she was aware of other women who alleged they were abused by Salah Fayed in Scotland, although some have never reported their experiences publicly.

She said she agreed with calls from some of the victims for a statutory public inquiry.

And she said she was speaking out because of worries the police investigations were not looking far enough.

Jill has contacted the Metropolitan Police and is also pursuing legal action.

Harrods, which is no longer owned by the Fayed family, said it recognised the "remarkable bravery" of survivors who had come forward and supported them in their pursuit of justice.

The retailer has previously established a redress scheme for survivors of abuse linked to Mohamed Al Fayed.

Jill said any compensation would be a partial refund for the impact on her life.

"You've lost years of your life," she said.

"You've had all these treatment costs, it's impacted your career, impacted your family, so yes they do need to put that right."

"The girl I was when I was sent to that man is gone," Jill said.

"I don't know who she would have been or what her life would have been like.

"My life's work has been recovering from this. It has been a bitter, bitter, decades-long struggle."

The BBC has contacted the Balnagown Estate for comment twice and as yet they have not replied.

item.title: Trump says immigration crackdown was 'too tough' and played part in midterms defeat
item.description: The president tells the CBS programme 60 Minutes he had been politically "hurt" by sweeping deportations.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump has said his immigration crackdown was "too tough", marking one of his clearest public retreats from a defining plank of his political agenda, following his party's drubbing in the midterm elections.

In an interview with CBS' 60 Minutes programme, Trump said he believed he deserved an "A plus" for drastically limiting illegal border crossings, but he had been politically "hurt" by sweeping deportations.

His acknowledgement came despite his homeland security department insisting it was not backing away from the crackdown.

Election day polling indicated immigration was the third most important issue for midterm voters, after the economy and the state of democracy.

In historically conservative states like Texas, a swing of Latino voters towards Democrats helped seal the Democratic Party's landslide majorities in Congress.

The president told 60 Minutes that immigration "both helped and hurt" his fellow Republicans in Tuesday's midterms.

"I think I got an A plus for closing up the border," he said in the programme that aired on Sunday evening.

He added: "For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out.

"But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally."

"I think it was too tough," the president said.

Trump also said he'd "love to do something on immigration" with congressional Democrats, without offering details.

In a previous interview with 60 Minutes a year ago, a defiant Trump insisted his administraiton's immigration raids "haven't gone far enough".

His conciliatory words on Sunday were an abrupt change in tone from a White House statement earlier in the day to the BBC.

A spokeswoman vowed "the administration will not slow down its efforts to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens who terrorise our communities".

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) also showed no sign of a U-turn on Sunday.

"ICE is NOT backing away or slowing down," a DHS spokesperson told the BBC.

Following Tuesday's electoral losses, Vice-President JD Vance had appeared receptive to adjusting their immigration strategy.

"I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement - by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labour, for instance," Vance wrote in a lengthy online post reflecting on the results.

However, Trump's promotion on Friday of immigration hawk Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff signalled no climbdown from the administration.

Miller is widely seen as the architect of the administration's hardline immigration policy during the first and second Trump presidencies.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) sources told CBS that in recent weeks officials have been instructed to aim for about 2,700 arrests of illegal immigrants per day, an increase from an earlier 2,000 daily arrest target.

Enforcement sweeps this year spurred anti-ICE demonstrations in cities including Chicago, Minneapolis and Los Angeles.

In Minneapolis, two US protesters, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were fatally shot by immigration agents.

item.title: Society needs to act to help white working-class pupils, inquiry says
item.description: The education secretary says she is backing the inquiry to "get to the heart of the barriers holding children back".
item.content:encoded:
Action from "across society" is needed to help improve the educational outcomes of white working-class children, the co-chair of an independent inquiry looking into the issue has said.

The inquiry's first report, published this summer, concluded that once-in-a-generation reforms were needed to fix a system "not serving the interests of white working-class children".

The next phase will focus on early years children and teenagers aged 14 to 19, aiming for a stronger start at primary school and improving older students' routes through education into successful careers.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was "backing" the inquiry to "get to the heart of the barriers holding children back".

Inquiry co-chair and former education secretary Baroness Morris said the next phase of the inquiry's work will consider "what needs to be done".

"This isn't just the responsibility of schools but calls for action from across society," she said.

The Independent Inquiry into White Working Class Educational Outcomes was commissioned by the multi-academy trust Star Academies, and is supported by the Department for Education.

It spoke to thousands of young people and their parents, as well as hundreds of teachers.

Education data about white working class pupils was also analysed as part of the year-long review, looking at the 1.25 million young people in England who are white British and in receipt of free school meals.

The inquiry found a growing belief among white working-class families that the current education system does not guarantee future success.

In the summer, the inquiry also acknowledged that the true scale of white working-class disadvantage is "likely to be substantially larger", as the education data they looked at did not include families who were on low incomes but did not receive free school meals.

Since then, all families receiving Universal Credit have become eligible for free school meals.

Under the new phase of the inquiry, practical recommendations for government, schools, colleges and other organisations working with white working-class communities will be developed.

This action will include a research programme looking at the routes taken by teenagers aged 14 to 19, investigating how schools can work with communities to provide clearer pathways into further study and successful employment.

The new phase of the inquiry will also look at how schools can ensure the transition from primary to secondary school builds strong foundations.

"Right now, too many white working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education," Powell said.

"That is why I am backing this independent inquiry to get to the heart of the barriers holding children back - from their first steps into school, through to the opportunities and choices they have as teenagers into further study, training or work."

It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced plans to open up new technical routes from age 14 in England over the summer.

The prime minister said he was "on a mission" to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training - known as "Neet".

Currently, nearly a million young people are classed as Neet.

Former minister Alan Milburn's interim report found that children who are not school-ready at aged four or five are nearly three times as likely to be Neet by ages 16 to 17.

A final report by Milburn is expected to set out his recommendations for tackling the issue in the coming weeks.

item.title: Inside the French drug gangs recruiting children to kill
item.description: The BBC enters Marseille's dangerous underworld, where young people are trapped, brutalised and exploited.
item.content:encoded:
Warning: Strong language and descriptions of sexual violence

Although she had just bought hashish from a drug dealer, the woman decided to call the police.

It was because, along with the illegal drugs, she had been handed a note by the young seller during their brief meeting on a Marseille housing estate in 2022.

"We're being held captive and need help. We are 15-years-old," it read.

The teenage dealer, a French court heard earlier this year, was one of two boys being held by a gang which they had both initially approached looking for paid work - albeit illegal.

One boy had been tasked with handling money, the other worked streets around the Frais-Vallon estate. Soon though, bosses had accused them of being responsible for "shortfalls" in takings.

What followed were regular beatings, the court was told, and being forced to dance naked in front of a camera as a form of blackmail. One of the boys was also raped.

Hours after the woman was passed the note, the two teenagers had tried to escape from a second-storey window, injuring themselves in the process. One managed to get away, while the other was caught, beaten and stabbed, but survived.

Arrests were made. Photos on the phone of one of the boys' alleged torturers showed several other young men in a similarly distressed condition. Six men have since been handed hefty sentences for what happened to the two teenagers.

The boys' story highlights the grip that drug gangs hold over parts of France's second city.

While the blend of Mediterranean culture, street art and hip-hop scene has made Marseille a popular tourist destination - beyond the city centre, it is another story.

After months of trying, a BBC team managed to enter this dangerous world - centred on deprived streets and high-rise housing estates in the port city, which police do not enter lightly.

We found an environment where ruthless gangs lure vulnerable young people with promises of easy money, but end up trapping them in a world of drug dealing, brutality and exploitation.

We saw how gangs use social media to recruit hitmen and spoke to several young men caught up in the violence. From prison, one gang member accused of involvement in several murders explained how his "cold-bloodedness" had helped him rise through the ranks.

The city's most powerful gang, DZ Mafia, emerged victorious from a bloody turf war and is now one of the most feared criminal organisations in France.

DZ is the official internet country code for Algeria, where one of the gang's founders, a French-Algerian called Mehdi Laribi, was detained earlier this year under a French arrest warrant.

The criminal outfit rose to prominence in 2023, when it became the first French gang to capitalise on its notoriety by releasing video statements - using social media to market itself as a brand - says the head of the country's anti-drug trafficking unit, Dimitri Zoulas.

Its most recent statement came in July, when the mayor of a nearby town had to be placed in police protection, after intelligence suggested he was in danger of being targeted by the group.

In an online video, six masked men dressed in black stood behind a table - as one of them read a statement denying DZ Mafia's involvement.

France's expanding illegal drugs market - which has seen a surge in cocaine imports alongside high volumes of cannabis and synthetic drugs - has also helped the gang grow rapidly.

The number of cocaine users in France is expected soon to reach two million, says Zoulas, up from 600,000 in 2017. Drug smuggling across France generates €7bn (£5.9bn) a year, involving 200,000 people, he adds.

Many of those distributing the drugs are children and the authorities say the number of minors caught up in trafficking is increasing. During 2025, more than 10,000 children were involved in some way, according to official figures.

DZ Mafia is a prime example. To reach more customers, it needs more gang members - more children.

We have found it is now recruiting young people from across France - not just to sell drugs, but to carry out kidnap, torture and murder.

They are a generation seen as easy to corrupt, but also expendable, by the kingpins who typically control them from prison or overseas.

And, as police and judges warn, once these children enter Marseille's underworld, it is very hard to get them out.

Few know the human cost of Marseille's gangs like mother Karine Brouillard - who lives at the other end of France, almost as far from the Mediterranean coast as you can get.

Her son, Hugo, first ran away aged 15 - from his home in a village in the Nord department - after an argument with his family. He was picked up by police three days later, almost 1,000km (600 miles) away in Marseille, with money and cannabis on him. He was taken home.

But several years later, in 2023, Hugo planned to return south, telling his parents he had secured a holiday job at a restaurant near Marseille.

"He gave regular updates," Karine remembers. "He called me, everything was going well."

Three weeks later, a doctor called. Karine says she will never forget his words: "Your son arrived last night. He took a bullet to the head."

Police believe Hugo was brought for medical help from a gang-controlled area and suspect he was involved with one.

That area was Quartier Nord.

Our best way into Quartier Nord, where DZ Mafia wields power, is with the help of resident Fadella Ouidef, a 41-year-old mother-of-four who gives us a tour.

Thirty-seven seconds after entering one housing estate, we find ourselves cornered.

Car horns sound the moment Fadella's Peugeot passes a gang checkpoint - the teenagers manning the post immediately spot our camera. "Wait, stop filming," Fadella warns, as a grey 4x4 forces us to the side of the road.

"I'm making a report for my housing association," she tells the inquisitive driver. He eventually agrees to let us leave if we stop filming.

It is unnerving to see a non-police vehicle move so assertively and a relief to watch it leave.

"Lately, the gangs have been very aggressive," explains Fadella. "What we simply try to do is make sure our young people understand what's happening is wrong."

Fadella speaks to a wider fear among local families: that their children are enticed by huge sums of money to take a criminal path that robs them of their innocence.

Money is what led one young man to spend his teenage years with DZ Mafia.

In order for our interviewees to speak freely, or because of safety concerns, we have agreed to protect their identities.

Camil tells us he worked up the gang's ranks to "running security" in one area it controls.

The now 20-year-old, who claims to have left the group, is highly suspicious of our presence, but agrees to tell us how the gang recruits young members.

"They know how to get inside your head. Whatever you want, they give to you," he says. This can range from nice cars and spacious apartments, to drugs and prostitutes, he explains.

"You feel loyalty because of what they give you. You'll stay until the very end, until either death or prison."

Camil also gives a sobering assessment of what happens if the gang identifies a weakness in a recruit: "They'll exploit it. You're their bitch, it's over."

DZ Mafia member, Adam - not his real name - tells us he was part of a DZ Mafia hit squad when we speak to him in a Snapchat video call.

He is currently in prison awaiting trial, after being implicated in several murders.

"People noticed my determination, my cold-bloodedness and, without wanting to, I climbed up the ladder of the gang," says Adam. "It became my place, I had to roll with it."

During the chat, he agrees the killings he has been charged with were "quite shocking".

"Attempts in broad daylight, in traffic jams… it can range from going to hit a guy, slap him to taking him in front of his mother and burning him up in a car. I think I have good composure, I handle it fairly well."

We challenge Adam on whether he feels regret when carrying out such acts of brutality.

He says he is "feeling in-part guilty" but claims to have no regrets.

"If I hadn't done all of this, there are other people who would have done that in my place, and so on. I am just another brick in the wall," he says.

Like so many teenagers from Marseille, he knew large sums of money could be earned quickly in drug trafficking. Now in his twenties, he admits the environment he entered was a "trap".

At a so-called deal point in a social housing estate - sealed off and controlled by DZ Mafia - price lists for cocaine, hashish and marijuana are graffitied on a wall.

The estate acts as a natural fortress for drug dealers. With one major road in and out, they can control the flow of customers and see if the police are coming.

It is not uncommon for the sound of automatic gunfire to fill the night air in these areas.

After months of negotiations, a deal-point manager from a rival gang agrees to meet us where he works.

We enter the estate early in the morning, the birdsong and children walking to school providing a stark contrast to the industrial-scale criminal operation that takes place here.

"Joe" says he was making €3,000 (£2,500) a month when he was 13. Now he says that has risen to between €5,000 and €10,000 a month.

He seems to see his life path as pre-ordained, albeit a lucrative one.

We ask Joe if he thinks about the lives lost because of the violence carried out by his gang, but the 23-year-old has also long made peace with the pain and destruction drug trafficking can cause.

"It destroys people, but we all make our own choices," he shrugs.

The work that Joe's gang and DZ Mafia are doing represents a threat to national security, says Zoulas, of the anti-drug trafficking unit.

There are road accidents, as well as family violence, depressions, suicides and more than 700 overdoses each year, he says, "and it distorts the economy".

"We are heading towards a potential systemic breakdown of the criminal justice system."

Police have had success in Marseille and other cities against drug gangs.

Criminal operations are being frustrated, more kingpins arrested and drugs seized.

Since 2024, about 1,000 individuals associated with DZ Mafia have been arrested, and 600 incarcerated, police say.

But overall, it is a battle that is becoming more arduous, rather than easier.

As gangs seek to widen their operations, or replace members who have been arrested or killed, social media has become a potent recruitment tool - especially since the Covid pandemic, when many street-drug sales jumped online.

On social media, we found countless posts advertising jobs in Marseille for aspiring drivers, couriers and hitmen, often with glamourised AI-generated images.

Nets are also being cast wider, as it becomes harder to entice young people locally because they know more about what might happen to them.

The ads can reach teenagers in most corners of France - including Paris, Nantes and Lille - and serve as a powerful pull to Marseille, and the Quartier Nord, police say.

Online advertising has also changed the typical profile of someone who would join a gang's ranks, say law enforcement officials.

Now, it is often someone without a criminal past, but who has exploitable vulnerabilities, like having a difficult family life.

"These people are recruited by unscrupulous sponsors who send them into the lion's den," explains Thibaut Fontaine, the head of France's anti-organised-crime unit.

Their lack of criminal experience, he says, makes them easier to arrest quickly.

Karine still has no idea why her son, Hugo, was shot.

Asked what she would say to gang leaders recruiting children and young men in Marseille, she says: "They destroy families. Little sisters, little brothers, grandparents. But then, I don't think those people have a heart, really."

The restaurant where her son said he was going to work did exist, but staﬀ there told Karine they had never recruited anyone called Hugo.

The reason for his death almost certainly lies within Marseille's Quartier Nord.

Additional reporting by Marianne Baisnee, Lea Guedj and Paul Pradier

item.title: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy
item.description: Jensen Huang also admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and says he will cooperate with a security investigation.
item.content:encoded:
US tech giant Nvidia has opened an independent investigation following reports its CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company, one of the most valuable in the world, said its board had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, adding that the CEO was committed to continuing to lead the company.

Separately, Jensen Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.

Jensen Huang said he took "full responsibility" for what he did, adding that he had fallen short of his responsibilities to Nvidia's employees, board and shareholders.

Nvidia is one of the world's largest companies and seen as central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, and Jensen Huang has been in charge of it for more than 30 years.

He said: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

His statement continued: "Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, Nvidia's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.

"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."

A separate statement issued by Nvidia's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

It continued: "The Board prioritises US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information."

US President Donald Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged.

"I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country".

Jensen Huang rescued Nvidia from almost going broke on more than one occasion, and he took a punt on AI a long time before the rest of the world did.

His decision to make Nvidia chips, originally designed for gaming, become the best in the business for AI development, has now paid off in spades and the company is worth trillions.

This is a big blow for a man who is renowned for being a workaholic, a perfectionist and someone who expects incredibly high standards from his staff.

Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, is linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed.

The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation.

Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, providing chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.

The microchip manufacturer is worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever.

China has previously rejected allegations of an espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".

US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.

Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".

It remains unclear what information Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.

Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.

Last week, members of Congress wrote to Jensen Huang, asking him to appear before them in the light of the reported relationship.

Three House Republican committee leaders asked the CEO to appear later in the month, to talk about Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage" given his reported relationship with Alice Huang.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information.

"The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the letter said.

Nvidia's AI chips have been a major focus of the rivalry between the US and China, and Washington has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

item.title: Aramco Tower hit in heart of Saudi capital as Houthis launch fresh strikes
item.description: Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows damage to the building in the capital's central financial district.
item.content:encoded:
The Aramco Tower, a skyscraper in the Saudi Arabian capital's central financial district, had been hit by an air attack.

A statement issued via the Houthi-controlled Saba news agency confirmed the group had targeted Riyadh's business zone on Saturday, without mentioning the Aramco Tower by name.

The Saudi energy ministry said the tower had suffered only "minor damage" and no one had been killed or injured.

Footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows more extensive damage to the building, with at least one floor appearing to have been badly hit by a missile or drone strike.

Windows on more than one level appear to have been shattered by the strike.

The Houthis also said Riyadh's airport and Aramco oil storage facilities were targeted in separate strikes. Saudi Arabia said its air defences had intercepted and destroyed several missiles.

The strikes were the latest claimed by the Yemen-based armed group against targets deep inside Saudi Arabia, which the Gulf power has struggled to contain in recent months.

It came a day after the Houthis accused a Saudi-led coalition of killing at least 33 people, including women and children, in an air strike on Yemen.

Footage broadcast by Houthi-run television channel Al Masirah showed rescuers pulling bodies from the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.

Saba said 39 people had been injured in the strike. Saudi Arabia has not commented.

A Saudi-led coalition has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government, which has lost control of a large swathe of the country to the rebel group.

Although the conflict had largely been dormant in recent years, fighting has intensified following the outbreak of the Iran war.

An informal ceasefire unravelled in July after the Tehran-backed Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport Saudi Arabia said had been to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing there.

Major fighting has since resumed between Houthi forces and troops aligned with Yemen's Saudi-backed government.

The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.

item.title: Top House Democrat 'a hard yes' on impeaching Hegseth
item.description: Democrats swept to power after historic midterm election success and are now eyeing the Trump administration for revenge.
item.content:encoded:
The lawmaker in pole position to lead the US House of Representatives after Democrats take control of Congress in January has said he is "a hard yes" for impeaching Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.

New York congressman Hakeem Jeffries told ABC programme This Week that Hegseth had "abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran".

Outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie, a foe of President Donald Trump, has said he plans to introduce a resolution to impeach Hegseth as early as Monday. The BBC asked the Pentagon for comment.

Congress returns to session this week after the Democrats' midterm elections landslide victory.

Massie's resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, including accusing him of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973 for America's role in the war with Iran.

"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," Jeffries told ABC on Sunday.

"Pete Hegseth has got to go," he continued.

Jeffries, who is favourite to be the next House Speaker, the most powerful member in the lower chamber of Congress, has vowed that the newly empowered Democrats will serve as a check and balance on the Trump administration.

But he said after the midterms results that House Democrats were not currently focused on impeaching President Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term.

Last week, Hegseth released a nearly six-minute video urging Congress to approve the Pentagon's latest military budget request, before the Republican-controlled legislature's final days come to an end.

In the clip, he addressed talks of Massie's impeachment effort, referring to the threat as "sham articles".

"You see, their policies don't work. So, their obsession with political theatre disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents," Hegseth said.

"It's all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn't work against President Trump and it won't work with me."

With more races still to be called, Democrats have a 254-seat majority in the House, well beyond the 218 threshold needed to pass articles of impeachment.

But they will fall well short of the two-thirds Senate majority required to remove an official from office.

item.title: Homes and temples glow across India to mark Diwali
item.description: Millions of Indians are marking the festival of lights with glowing lamps, fireworks and traditional sweets.
item.content:encoded:
Millions across India are celebrating Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness.

The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky.

Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers.

But the celebrations come amid growing concerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India.

Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse.

Air pollution in the Indian capital Delhi has reached such hazardous levels that it is the most polluted Diwali festival in a decade. New measures to improve air quality do not seem to have been successful.

India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks.

In an effort to limit pollution, India's Supreme Court on Monday permitted the manufacture, sale and use of certified "green" firecrackers in Delhi and surrounding areas for a limited period.

These firecrackers are designed to produce 20-30% fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. But critics have questioned how effective they are at reducing pollution and raised concerns that conventional firecrackers could still make their way into the capital from neighbouring states.

Despite the debate over fireworks, Diwali is about much more than firecrackers.

The festival celebrates the return of Lord Ram to Ayodhya after his victory over Ravan, the main antagonist in the Hindu epic Ramayana, and symbolises the triumph of good over evil, light over darkness, and knowledge over ignorance.

In the days leading up to the festival, families clean and decorate their homes with flowers, colourful lights and traditional oil lamps known as diyas.

The celebrations also bring families and friends together for prayers, elaborate feasts and the exchange of gifts, and lots of traditional Indian sweets.

Colourful patterns known as rangoli are created at entrances to homes, while markets bustle with shoppers buying festive essentials beneath brightly lit decorations.

The celebrations began on 6 November with Dhanteras, when buying gold, silver or new utensils is considered auspicious and believed to bring good fortune.

The second day, known as Chhoti Diwali, or small Diwali, is marked by the lighting of oil lamps and, in some households, setting off firecrackers.

The third day is the main celebration, when families offer evening prayers to Lakshmi, the Hindu goddess of wealth and prosperity, before gathering for festive meals and fireworks.

The fourth day is celebrated differently across India, with family gatherings and New Year festivities in some communities. The fifth and final day, known as Bhai Dooj, celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters.

The festival is also celebrated by Sikhs and Jains along with other important religious observances.

Sikhs mark Bandi Chhor Divas, or Prisoner Release Day, commemorating the release of their sixth guru, Guru Hargobind, from imprisonment at Gwalior Fort in the early 17th Century.

For Jains, Diwali marks the attainment of moksha, or liberation from the cycle of rebirth, by Lord Mahavira, the 24th and last Tirthankara, or spiritual teacher, of the current era.

With Indian communities spread across the world, Diwali is also celebrated internationally, with families and friends coming together for festive gatherings and exchanging gifts.

The festival is considered an auspicious time to make new purchases, which many believe bring prosperity and good fortune. India's stock exchanges even hold a special one-hour trading session for investors who consider buying and selling shares on Diwali favourable. Known as Muhurat trading, it will take place on 8 November this year.

Although rooted in Hindu traditions, Diwali is celebrated by people across different faiths and communities.

item.title: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
item.description: Several carriages derailed after two trains travelling in the same direction crashed outside the city of Giza.
item.content:encoded:
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.

The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.

Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.

Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".

The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.

The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.

Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.

The Egyptian Red Crescent said it was providing aid and psychological support to victims and their families at the scene.

The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.

The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.

Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.

Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains. The railway authority has not said how long it expects this to take.

The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.

In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.

Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.

There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.

Foreign leaders and dignitaries have shared condolences and support for the victims.

Saudi Arabia's ministry of foreign affairs expressed "solidarity" with Egypt and wished those hurt a speedy recovery.

Turkey's ambassador to Egypt wrote on X that he extended "heartfelt condolences and sincere sympathy" to the victims, their families, and the Egyptian people.

item.title: Surgeon having lunch near Krakow shooting undoubtedly saved officer's life, colleague says
item.description: One of the men, Professor Michal Pędziwiatr, when they got to the scene, they treated both the alleged gunman and the police officers.
item.content:encoded:
One of the two surgeons who rushed to save lives in the aftermath of a mass shooting in Poland says his colleague stopped the bleeding of the police officer, "undoubtedly" saving his life.

Professor Michal Pędziwiatr and Dr Mateusz Wierdak were having lunch in central Krakow with their families when they heard gunshots, local media reports.

"Suddenly my son ran up and said: 'Dad, they're shooting at people there, people are falling to the ground'," Pędziwiatr told news outlet Fakt.

Pędziwiatr said when they got to the scene, they treated both the apparent attacker and the police officers.

"When it comes to saving lives, it doesn't matter who is who."

Police are continuing to investigate Saturday's incident after six people were killed in the Krakow's market square. Sixteen more were injured, including Senior Police Constables Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański.

Three other bodies were found in the alleged gunman's apartment who were identified by police as the suspect's parents and sister.

Once the shooting stopped, Pędziwiatr said he took care of the other victims and the apparent perpetrator who needed help, while Wierdak began working on the police officer who was shot in the chest during the gunfight.

"He, to put it colloquially, stuffed all the bandages into [the police officer's] chest and stuck his hands in," he told Fakt.

"If not for that, I don't know how things would have turned out, as there was a long wait for the ambulance".

Meanwhile, Pędziwiatr said he called John Paul II Hospital where the Department of Thoracic and Cardiac Surgery is located.

"I insisted they take him there because, in my opinion, he had the best chance of survival there, where there were specialists for precisely this type of injury," he told Fakt.

According to local media, Wierdak is a renowned surgeon in Krakow. The University Hospital in Krakow states Pędziwiatr is head of General, Oncological, Metabolic and Emergency Surgery.

Four women and two men were among those killed, including four polish nationals, a British man and a non-Polish citizen whose nationality has not yet been disclosed.

The National Public Prosecutor's Office in Poland is launching an investigation into the attack with a unit specialising in "terrorist offences" taking the lead.

Separately, six Dublin Civil Defence volunteers reportedly also assisted in the aftermath of the shooting.

James McConnell, an officer, told RTE News the group were on a city break and were close to the main square when the shooting happened.

The volunteers who are trained to provide medical care immediately sought to help injured people, providing "CPR and haemorrhage control".

item.title: Can the Zelda remake capture the magic of the original?
item.description: Nintendo has released its remake of what is considered one of the best games ever made - the BBC's Tom Gerken gives his verdict.
item.content:encoded:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was finally released on Thursday, after years of rumours that Nintendo would remake the game - considered one of the best ever made.

IGN called it "the biggest game of the decade" in their review when it launched in 1998 on the N64, and it set the standard for 3D games.

A lot of the things we take for granted in modern games - such as riding a horse, fighting with a sword and shield, or locking on to enemies with the tap of a button - were pioneered or perfected in Ocarina of Time.

It received an almost perfect score from critics and, decades on, remains the highest-rated game in history on Metacritic, which aggregates reviews.

So how do you remake what many consider a masterpiece?

Those like me who grew up playing the original will feel right at home here.

Nintendo has decided against reinventing the wheel, instead producing something which plays very similarly to the N64 classic.

As I've said before, video game remakes are a bit different to film or TV - gaming fans often clamour for a new take on their favourites, hoping developers harness evolution in tech to make them fresh.

And games have come a long way in the almost 30 years since the original Ocarina of Time came out.

"When you compare the games in the past and the games in modern times, so to speak, the norms of what people expect from a game have evolved naturally," Nintendo producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi told me.

"In the past, games where the users may have needed more imagination to fill the blanks or the gaps are now clearly expressed through the graphics that they see on the screen."

But fancy graphics have come at a price - a pivot away from realism into something a bit more cartoonish. Some might even be disappointed by this, given the N64 game had quite horrifying elements in places.

One was the Skulltula House, a room where people had been morphed into human-spider hybrids.

"Back when we created the original Ocarina of Time, the means to convey or express ideas was limited compared with what we have now," series producer Eiji Aonuma - who worked on the original game - said.

"With regard to even the so-called scary elements, we strove to add a touch of the comical."

But he told the BBC that enhanced graphics and lighting capabilities unintentionally exaggerated the already-spooky Skulltula House and its potential to strike fear into players.

"When we carried out the test play, the testers were telling us, 'Oh, this is too scary'," he said. "So of course, in the end product, we've made the necessary adjustments so that we can retain the same balance that we had achieved in the original."

'Serious thought has gone into every decision'

I spoke to a few YouTubers about the upcoming game to get their thoughts - and the response was overwhelmingly positive.

Mike Channell, co-editor of the YouTube channel Outside Xbox, said he believed the remake had been made "very meticulously" in the hopes of living up to fan expectations.

"Having played the game, it's clear that serious thought has gone into every decision, to the point where I'm not convinced this remake has taken any less time and effort than an all-new Zelda game," he said.

"Ocarina of Time is obviously one of the great video game experiences in the history of the medium, but I have no doubt this new version will be the best way to experience this story.

"It's fleshed out as a world, sumptuously detailed, and the controls match 21st-Century expectations."

Ed King, known as Zeltik to his 893,000 followers on YouTube, said "the level of detail and charm" in the Ocarina of Time remake stood out.

"The Forest Temple has always been my favourite Zelda dungeon: a mysterious, haunted mansion in the deep woods, a lost work of man slowly being reclaimed by nature," he said. "The remake really leans into the surreal, uncanny nature of the original dungeon."

And fellow YouTuber StrawHatMidas said it was the "perfect" way to "bring this classic back".

"Not only does the game pay homage to the Nintendo 64 original, but it also expands on the things that made it so memorable," he said. "Everything from the world and atmosphere to the controls and soundtrack feels like a love letter to the classic Zelda formula."

Has Nintendo played it too safe?

Nintendo has made some big changes, not least to the Water Temple - a dungeon about two thirds into the game.

Aonuma said, having worked on the original, this was what he personally wanted to change most due to its reputation for being "very, very difficult".

He said there was now "a greater facility in tackling" the dungeon, as players can now easily change a critical in-game item known as heavy boots and have "the ability to leverage the camera orientation".

I grew up playing Zelda on the N64, which pioneered the joystick - but nowadays two sticks is the standard, with one to move and one to control the camera.

As far as I'm concerned, being able to freely move the camera this time round was a significant improvement.

At times, the trip down memory lane was captivating. I knew where to go and what to do, thanks to a kind of muscle memory. However, on occasion that took away from the experience - with some tasks achieved too easily and some puzzles too quickly because I recalled their solutions.

Some people will love how similar it is, but I have to wonder if Nintendo has played things a bit too safe.

I don't think the developers see it that way.

"Even if the game may look different, we've maintained the essence that the original developers wanted to and hopefully conveyed through the original Ocarina of Time," Fujibayashi said.

Don't get me wrong - the game has lots of changes and surprises, and I won't spoil them, but I wish there had been more.

Then again, perhaps the best games leave you wanting more.

Or as Mike put it: "I loved the original as much as the next person, but I don't think I'll be going back to it."

Fans will no doubt wonder whether this is it, or if there will be more Zelda on the horizon. With the franchise's first movie coming next year, there's certainly more to come in the short term.

And in the long term, I wondered if with 30 more years of technological advancements, Nintendo might consider remaking the game once again.

"I will be long retired," Aonuma said, with a laugh.

Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletter to follow the world's top tech stories and trends. Outside the UK? Sign up here.

item.title: He spent $50,000 on Labubus but now the craze is dying
item.description: Parent company Pop Mart's revenue has fallen as appetite for the quirky collectible monsters wanes.
item.content:encoded:
For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.

Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (£11) or more.

Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market.

The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases.

Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say".

He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events.

But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now."

Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies.

It's a sign that the craze which made parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put together may be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment.

Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year.

The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%.

The rise and fall

Pop Mart didn't invent blind boxes but its dolls certainly helped to popularise them around the world.

The sales tactic made collecting feel "nostalgic", evoking the feeling of opening gifts as a child, says marketing professional Katelynn Carlson, who discovered Labubus through social media and now owns 36 of them.

One of her first Labubus was a rare doll, making the experience "even more exciting", she adds.

Labubu, which launched in 2019, has been Pop Mart's most successful line of toys. The monsters became fashion statements and were sported by celebrities including Kim Kardashian and Blackpink's Lisa.

They regularly attracted long queues and became so popular that Pop Mart had to temporarily pull the toys from its UK shops after reports of customers fighting over them. One fan paid more than $150,000 for a human-sized Labubu.

A key part of the allure was how difficult some Labubu dolls were to find, with fans repeatedly buying blind boxes to get the version they wanted, says National University of Singapore marketing lecturer Samer El Hajjar.

Pop Mart now has 500 shops in more than 30 countries and 2,000 vending machines worldwide. The firm, which listed in Hong Kong in 2020, is worth nearly $24bn and remains one of the world's most valuable toymakers, despite its shares having fallen by more than 50% from last year's peak.

Investors worry its global success was just a viral moment rather than sustainable growth driven by long-term customer loyalty, El Hajjar says.

For Ensito, it is clear the dolls' exclusivity helped fuel the craze.

"Now it doesn't feel that way. I walk into a Pop Mart and there's a whole series of Labubus sitting there," he says.

Ashley Dudarenok of China research firm ChoZan says that sense of exclusivity faded as Pop Mart ramped up production to meet demand.

Pop Mart declined to comment on share price moves and did not respond to questions about falling sales.

Rivals take over

As the Labubu mania cools, some of its rivals have become more popular.

Blind box collectables like Sonny Angels - tiny, unclothed cherub-like dolls - and miniature glow-in-the-dark Smiski figurines have been flying off shelves. And you can now find My Little Pony and KPop Demon Hunters in blind boxes too.

Miniso, founded in the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou, sells a range of blind-boxed Disney and Marvel characters in more than 8,000 shops globally.

"Consumers aren't particularly concerned about where the brand comes from," Miniso executive Vincent Huang said earlier this year. "They're more focused on the shopping experience - the designs, value for money, and enjoyment."

Experts say one of Pop Mart's biggest challenges is creating enduring characters.

That's an area where Hello Kitty brand Sanrio, which posted record earnings in the year to March, has a clear advantage, analyst Boustani suggests.

Pop Mart has invested heavily in ways to grow its brand, including setting up a theme park in Beijing and announcing a Labubu film - following in the footsteps of franchising giants like Disney or Lego, some experts believe.

But unlike Disney, which sells a story before it sells a toy, Pop Mart is working in reverse, says Dudarenok. "The real test for next year is whether Pop Mart can make people love a character without a celebrity holding it."

'Now I only buy what I like'

After spending huge sums on the monsters, collector Ensito says he is now questioning how much time and money people invest in collections each time a new trend comes along. "There's always going to be a trend every year. There's always gonna be something that's gonna be really popular."

Melbourne-based content creator Lawrence Yu says that after two years of chasing Labubus, he's likely to be "more selective" before adding to his roughly 50 dolls.

His Labubu shopping and unboxing clips once drew up to a million views but the frenzy has faded and Yu rarely makes videos about them now. "I definitely think the trend has slowed down... People go crazy and then it fizzles."

Clara Barbero from Canada believes Labubus are a "dead trend" but is still keeping an eye out for interesting releases.

"I’m curating my collection more and only buying what I see myself liking for the next few years, and not just buying the newest series that’s out."

But the fluffy monsters still have truly devoted fans.

Hedy Khaled from Liverpool says although the hype around the dolls is cooling, she is just as attached to her collection of 70 Pop Mart figurines.

There's a distinction between those who chase trends and "real fans", she argues, so falling sales do not necessarily mean Labubus have lost their appeal.

For Carlson says it is the happiness the dolls bring, not the viral trend, that keeps her collecting. She still gets excited about new Pop Mart releases, like its recent cat-themed Labubu series, which has become one of her favourites.

"I think there's something special about embracing our inner child and enjoying things simply because they make us happy."

item.title: King leads solemn Remembrance Sunday service at Cenotaph
item.description: Wreaths are laid as 10,000 armed forces veterans, including 12 from World War Two, pay tribute in central London.
item.content:encoded:
King Charles III led the nation in a solemn two-minute silence on Remembrance Sunday in London to honour veterans who had died in conflict.

On a stone-grey autumn morning, he laid a wreath at the Cenotaph in Whitehall before a march-past by 10,000 armed forces veterans.

That included a shrinking number of World War Two veterans, with 12 taking part this year, including 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who described it as a "very emotional day".

Meanwhile, the number of former prime ministers reached a record high, with nine lined up to lay wreaths, while Andy Burnham attended for the first time as the current occupant of No 10 Downing Street.

And for the first time, the leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, had enough MPs in Parliament to qualify to lay a wreath alongside other major party leaders.

The Prince of Wales and the Princess Royal were among royals in attendance, along with military chiefs, senior politicians, diplomats and faith leaders, watched by big crowds squeezed behind railings along Whitehall.

Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales watched from a balcony above the Cenotaph in the Foreign Office.

Among the flags on the roof of that Whitehall building was the Ukrainian blue and yellow. It went up when Russia invaded and four years later it is now visibly frayed - a reminder of the length of that war and of current threats.

At 11:00 GMT, as the first strike of Big Ben echoed from the nearby Houses of Parliament, the big two-minute silence filled the usually frenetic streets, before the playing of the Last Post.

The King had his eyes closed, the crowds in Whitehall stopped for their own thoughts, in a rare moment of calm in the capital.

The poignant parade past the Cenotaph included representatives of about 340 different military and civilian groups, from the Royal Naval Association and the Royal Marines Association to Transport for London and the Royal National Lifeboat Institute.

Alongside those marching were flotillas of disability scooters and families helping veterans in wheelchairs.

Those who took part in WW2 are now increasingly frail - and there were 12 participants in the march-past compared to 20 last year. The oldest participant this year was aged 105.

Taking part for the first time was 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who had been part of the Land Army that had helped to feed the country at war.

She had joined the Land Army in 1940 as a 16-year-old, having lied about her age, and worked on a farm in Leicestershire.

"I feel very honoured to be taking part in the parade and to represent the Land Girls. I'm very excited, although a little apprehensive as I don't quite know what to expect," she said.

"I think it will be a very emotional day, bringing back memories of all those who didn't return home. It will be lovely to be there and remember them."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the annual event was a time to "reflect on the selflessness and courage it takes to commit your life to protecting others".

He earlier announced that he wanted to tackle the problem of homelessness among ex-service personnel to "ensure that any veteran sleeping rough is offered appropriate accommodation before Christmas".

Mark Atkinson, the director general of the Royal British Legion, said: "As we come together on Remembrance Sunday, we pay tribute to all those who have served and sacrificed, from generations past to those still serving today."

For more than a century, this national Remembrance event has been held around the Cenotaph.

The monument was built as a focal point for honouring those who had fought and died in World War One, including those who had no grave, and as a place to mourn for those families who might not be able to visit war cemeteries overseas.

The word "cenotaph" means "empty tomb" in Greek and it was designed by the architect Sir Edwin Lutyens in a simple, austere style, with no sense of triumphalism and with almost no decoration.

The monument had been originally built in 1919 as a temporary, plaster and wood structure. But it proved so popular with the public that it was replaced in 1920 with a permanent version, in the same design but in stone.

It was opened at 11:00 on 11 November 1920 by King George V. His great-grandson, Charles, was there again, on an overcast morning 106 years later, to continue paying respect.

item.title: Six killed in Krakow 'far-right' shooting, as three more bodies found in attacker's home
item.description: Police say the Polish attacker drove into a popular square in the city's centre and began randomly firing at people.
item.content:encoded:
A gunman believed to have been inspired by far-right ideology has killed six people and injured more than a dozen others in an attack in the busy centre of Poland's second largest city.

Police said the attacker drove onto Main Market Square in Krakow, a popular tourist attraction, on Saturday afternoon and began randomly firing at people.

The attacker, who was equipped with military-style weapons and attire, was injured in a gunfight with police, one of whom was critically injured in the process.

The 25-year-old Polish man - described by one minister as "ultra-nationalist" - has been taken to hospital for surgery.

Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said another three bodies were found during a search of the suspect's home around 125 miles (200km) away from Krakow.

Tusk said there were "strong indications" the two women and one man were the suspect's immediate family members.

He said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism... that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."

Four women and two men were killed in the square. Three were Polish, one was British and two have not been identified, officials said.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "I'm shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in Kraków today."

"My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added.

The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in the historic centre of Krakow, an ornate square which has long been a draw for tourists.

Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out.

The glass front of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes.

Images from the scene showed overturned tables and scattered belongings left behind as people ran for their lives.

Armed police officers pursued the attacker's car until it crashed, at which point they engaged him in a firefight.

Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify captured the moment a police officer confronted the suspect as he lay on the ground.

The officer, who is visibly injured, can then be seen falling to the ground.

A Polish minister later said one police officer was fighting for his life and a second was expected to recover from a less serious injury.

Tusk later named them as Senior Constable Jakub Kulik and Senior Constable Artur Morański - he said they "saved many lives" and called them "true heroes".

The gunman wore full military tactical gear during the attack and was described as having a military-grade weapon - but the government said he was not a member of the Polish armed forces.

More weapons and ammunition were found in a car belonging to the suspect, whose name has not been confirmed.

Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said "everything suggests that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held "ultra-nationalist views".

Tusk vowed that any "possible supporters of the perpetrator" would be detained and appealed to the public for information.

A massive armed police presence was deployed across Krakow on Saturday evening, as security measures were ramped up in the capital Warsaw and elsewhere.

Of the 15 injured, two were police officers and five were foreign nationals - the interior ministry said they were from Britain, Austria, Russia, Germany and Portugal.

European foreign policy chief Kaja ⁠Kallas called it "a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland."

British foreign secretary Ed Miliband said on social media the UK government "deeply mourns" those who died in the "appalling attack".

"All of my deepest condolences go to the families of the victims," he added.

The Foreign Office updated its advice after the attack and said people in the area should follow the advice of local authorities.

Witnesses who were close to the attack described panic and confusion around the square as it unfolded.

Cezary, a 24-year-old Polish university student in Krakow, said he did not realise the loud bangs he heard were gunshots until he saw four bodies lying on the street.

"We were still hearing gunshots, a lot of people were screaming," he said, adding that he saw someone trying to resuscitate a person covered in blood on the ground.

Caitlin Shasby, from Newcastle in the UK, said she heard shooting from her hotel room and was told to take shelter inside as police "barricaded" the street outside.

Another witness told Polish news website Inertia: "I saw shots being fired from the driver's side window and smoke was coming out.

"I ran to the police station in the main market square - when I burst inside, it was full of people hiding on the floor."

A period of mourning has been declared in Krakow until 11 November.

item.title: My parents chose to die together and I was left to grieve alone
item.description: Jan and Els sought medical intervention to end their lives together after 50 happy years of marriage, leaving behind their only child.
item.content:encoded:
Some people might find this article upsetting.

Early one morning in June 2024, Bas pulled up next to his parents' campervan, parked on a sunny marina in the north of the Netherlands.

His father and mother, Jan and Els, had spent most of their married life on water. Now in their 70s, they could no longer manage a houseboat. Their campervan, positioned close to the yachts and dinghies, was the next best thing.

Jan and Els got into their son's car. Bas started the engine. This would be the final time he drove his parents anywhere. For Jan and Els, this journey - to the local hospice - would be their last.

At 10:30 that morning they would be administered lethal medication by doctors and die together in what is known in the Netherlands as duo-euthanasia. It's legal and it's rare, but every year more Dutch people choose to end their lives this way.

Three days before their fatal appointment at the hospice, Jan and Els gave an interview to the BBC in their campervan. Jan was living with continual pain, the legacy of years hauling cargo on the Netherlands' inland waterways. Els had been diagnosed with dementia. Their story was picked up and commented on around the world.

Now, more than two years on, the couple's only child describes trying to persuade his mother and father to delay their deaths while supporting their decision to stop living. He reveals the emotional burden his parents' decision placed on him and the profound loneliness that followed.

The journey

Bas had planned a scenic route to the hospice, taking in Friesland's meadows and canals.
