item.title: Scientists detect signals at the smallest scale ever explored
item.description: Researchers have detected signals from the smallest distances ever probed.
item.content:encoded:
Scientists have picked up signals from the smallest scale of nature ever explored – 100 billion times smaller than an atom.

A world so small that some physicists have nicknamed it the zeptoverse.

The research, led by scientists based in Cambridge, was obtained from an experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

This vast machine at the European Laboratory for Particle Physics (Cern) on the Swiss-French border smashes atoms together to break them apart and discover what is inside them.

The result is important because it could help researchers develop a new, more complete theory of how the Universe works.

'Knocking on the door' of the zeptoverse

Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.

Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.

So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions.

One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.

The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.

Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.

Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter.

"We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News.

He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles.

"And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.

The 28 countries involved in the project have agreed a £150m upgrade to this detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHCb), which would increase the frequency of these decays tenfold.

"With that we can probe inside the zeptoverse and see what's waiting," Cliff said.

But last year the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) agency, the government body in charge of research funding, announced that it was withdrawing its share of the money for the planned upgrade.

It later announced cuts to several other particle physics and astronomy projects this Summer, including Jodrell Bank's iconic Lovell telescope.

Although this research was led by scientists based in Cambridge, because of the cuts, Prof Tim Gershon, who leads the LHCb international collaboration, told BBC News that the UK's full involvement in the research would be in doubt.

"The UK is at risk of not being involved and making really major discoveries," he told BBC News.

"But I think the biggest long-term impact comes from the fact that the UK won't get the benefits from training young people who really are our greatest product."

Among those early-career researchers is Dr Mary Richardson-Slipper, who is part of the team that made the zeptoverse discovery. She is reconsidering her future in light of the physics cuts.

"I love being here in the UK, but I am looking at jobs abroad because that seems to be where there are more opportunities at the moment," said Richardson-Slipper.

She added that "lots" of her fellow researchers working in fundamental physics had already moved.

The cuts are being made despite an overall record increase in the science budget.

Prof Brian Cox, TV presenter and particle researcher at the University of Manchester, who is not part of the research team, described the result as "important".

But he condemned the recent decision to cut UK funding for the Cern project.

"It would be extraordinary to walk away from UK scientific leadership at this moment, damaging the future research programme and seriously damaging our hard-won international reputation," Cox said.

The UKRI told BBC News that it remained a fully engaged member of Cern as its second largest funder at around £175m per year.

A UKRI spokesperson said: "We sought independent advice and have taken forward an exciting portfolio of new infrastructure investments, which include projects in clean energy, medical imaging and cultural heritage.

"However, as usual, there were more exciting applications for funding than we were able to support."

item.title: When will we know the US midterms results?
item.description: Once polls close, it is possible the results will not be projected for several hours, days or even weeks
item.content:encoded:
Millions of Americans are voting in midterm elections that could reshape the balance of power in Washington. The outcome determines which party - US President Donald Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress.

Once polls close, it is possible the results will not be projected for several hours, days or even weeks. Here's what you need to know.

When will we know the results and who controls Congress?

Congress is made up of two parts - the lower chamber, the House of Representatives and the upper chamber, the Senate.

To win a majority in the House, a party needs 218 seats. In the Senate, a party needs 51 seats for an outright majority. But if the upper chamber is split 50-50, the vice-president has a tie-breaking vote, which gives their party control of it.

First results will start to come in after 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT). They won't tell us much about the overall result because these races are in places considered safe bets for Republicans (Kentucky and Indiana) or Democrats (Vermont).

Throughout the night, BBC analysts will focus on the competitive races which will give an indication of how well things are going for Trump.

There are several tight Senate contests in the Eastern Time zone - like Ohio, where polls close at 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) and Maine, where they shut at 20:00 EST (01:00 GMT). These could provide early indications of the electorate's mood.

Some key contests might start to be "called" by US media outlets. They use models to project which way a state has voted, even before the full vote count has been completed.

This happens when they believe a party or a candidate has gained a lead that cannot be beaten. But in some closely-fought states, outlets could take a long time to make their projections.

The overall timing of the result will depend on how tight the races are and which races end up being decisive.

When did we know the results in 2022?

In 2022, Republicans and Democrats were still in a tight race for control of the US Congress on 9 November, a day after the midterms.

While Republicans were favourites to win the House of Representatives, the fight for the Senate remained on a knife-edge.

The full picture took several days. CBS News projected Republicans had secured the 218 seats needed for a majority in the House on 17 November.

Counting in a crucial Senate race in Nevada took four days. The Democrats' narrow victory in the state brought them to 50 seats, allowing them to retain control of the Senate because then Vice-President Kamala Harris held a tie-breaking vote.

Georgia's Senate contest had to be settled by a run-off election because no candidate passed the 50% mark in November.

The results were not available until 7 December, when Democrats won this seat.

What are the key races to watch in 2026?

There are seven Senate races deemed to be a toss-up by independent elections analyst Cook Political Report - Alaska, Kansas, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas.

Of these, six are currently held by Republicans and one by Democrats. The Democrats would need to win four of those seats, plus four classed as likely or leaning Democratic, to hit 51 and take control of the Senate.

If Democrats fail to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, winning a majority in the Senate becomes much harder. Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, is up against Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent.

But polls have suggested they have a chance even in Texas where former teacher James Talarico could become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the state since 1988 if he defeats Ken Paxton, the current state attorney general and close Trump ally.

The current Republican majority in the House, the lower chamber, is thin. They have 218 representatives, the exact number needed to have control, plus one independent who votes with them.

Some of the most closely-watched races in the House are in east-coast states, according to the Cook Political Report. These include New York's 17th District, Pennsylvania's 8th District and Virginia's 1st District.

When do polls close?

The results of a voter poll will be released at 17:00 EST (22:00 GMT), which will give us an indication of the issues at the forefront of voters' minds.

Then, at 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT), the first polls close in Kentucky and Indiana. After that, all eyes will be focused on the seven key battleground states:

  • 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) - Polls close in Ohio, where Republican Senator Jon Husted finds himself neck-and-neck with Democrat Sherrod Brown. Results from this state could give us a clue as to how the night might unfold
  • 20:00 EST (01:00 GMT) - Voting ends in the tight Senate race in Maine between Republican Senator Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson and in most of Michigan, Kansas and Texas
  • 21:00 EST (02:00 GMT) - Polls close in Iowa and the remaining parts of Michigan that sit in the Central Time Zone, as well as Kansas and Texas. In the hours that follow, a picture might start to emerge of whether things are going to plan for the Republicans - or the Democrats
  • 01:00 EST (06:00 GMT) - Voting ends in Alaska, the last battleground state. A close Senate race between Democrat Mary Peltola and incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan has been making headlines over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot

How does the vote-counting work?

Each state administers its own elections and has its own rules for counting and processing votes.

The order of which votes are tallied first varies from state to state. Some states, like Florida, process early and mail ballots prior to election day, while others only begin tabulating on 3 November.

Local election officials - sometimes appointed, sometimes elected - verify, process and count individual votes, in a process known as canvassing.

Most states require a formal post-election audit that involves a manual count of ballots checked against machine totals, although rules vary across the country. Full hand counts are generally reserved for recounts.

Every state and locality has rigorous rules which specify who can participate in the canvass, the order in which votes are processed and which parts are open to the public, including how partisan observers can watch the count and, in some states, raise formal challenges.

What might cause a delay?

Tight races will take longer, and create the possibility of recounts being triggered and legal challenges.

Mail-in ballots take considerably longer to count, as officials need to process envelopes and verify signatures.

More than 30 states allow ballots to be processed before election day, but other states do not, meaning that it may take days to get results.

In California, all ballots must be posted before or on election day and will still be counted if they arrive within seven days of the election.

As every state has its own rules and policies, some delays could be built-in to the system.

In Alaska, ranked-choice voting could mean that tabulations take considerably longer than elsewhere in the country and the controversy over ballots could mean that legal challenges can complicate things.

What happens if results are challenged?

Once every vote has been included in the final results, and after processes such as recounts have been completed, the election results are certified - first at the local, county, level. The results are then certified state-wide, usually by a state canvassing board of the secretary of state.

The governor then typically signs the certifications for House and Senate winners to be sent to Congress.

Results can be challenged. Recounts can be requested by candidates in close races, and in some states recounts are automatically triggered if they fall within a certain margin.

Additionally, candidates can file legal election contests alleging irregularities.

Congress has the final word. Losing candidates in both House and Senate races can file contests, with slightly different processes in each of the two chambers.

Both chambers can, theoretically, refuse to seat someone or order an investigation.

When do winners take office?

Outgoing members of Congress leave office on Sunday 3 January. Because that date falls on a weekend, the new members may take office on the same date unless Congress passes a law setting a different day.

Additional reporting by James FitzGerald, Yazmina García-Fernández, Tom Geoghegan and Mike Hills.

item.title: Americans head to the polls for elections that could define Trump's closing chapter
item.description: The midterms will shape Congress for the last years of his presidency, writes Sarah Smith, but they are also a test of what politics may look like without him.
item.content:encoded:
With two years of his presidency remaining, Donald Trump, who has dominated American politics over the past decade and transformed it in remarkable ways, is facing potentially pivotal elections.

And the midterm elections on Tuesday that will decide control of Congress come at a difficult moment for his Republican Party.

Voters overwhelmingly say they are most concerned about the cost of living. Food and fuel prices have soared in part due to the president's aggressive tariffs and unpopular war with Iran, so it will be top of mind as many head to the polls.

Trump, who has faced record low approval ratings in recent months, has been campaigning hard, headlining dozens of rallies across the country.

He made his closing pitch on Monday in front the Reflecting Pool in Washington DC, which has been the subject of a controversial renovation. Looking back at the midterms campaign, he said Republicans "gave this a very strong shot".

But ahead of the vote, high prices are a concern for voters on all sides - which helps explain why he has been campaigning in previously safe Republican territory, appearing in Iowa and Kansas during a final weekend blitz.

His party has also poured hundreds of millions of dollars of campaign advertising into these traditionally safe contests, such as the Senate race in Kansas.

"When they start spending hard American dollars on political advertising in a state that they should be winning, that's how you know that they think they're in trouble," Carrie Dann, the managing editor of the Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, told the BBC.

"The spending [in Kansas] is going to be far more than Republicans ever anticipated," she added. That points to a party that is approaching these elections on the defensive.

At many of his rallies, Trump has also made a plea to voters. "In this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot," he said last month. "Just pretend."

Of course, he is not on the ballot. But this plea - which he made again in Iowa on Sunday - gets to the heart of a critical question: Is he still an electoral asset for his Republican Party?

The answer to that is not as simple as it once was.

Trump returned to the White House as a formidable force following his crushing 2024 election win - and had the healthy approval ratings to match. Before that, during the previous midterm elections in 2022, his endorsement was courted by Republicans who saw it as vital to success.

Now, with the war with Iran dragging on and hitting many Americans in the pocket, his approval ratings have sunk. The price of a gallon of diesel - which was $3.75 before the war started in February - hit a record high of $6.52 in September.

"I literally just had my son drive across the country, and he called me in every state and told me the price of gas," one voter in Iowa told me. "And I was like - 'oh my gosh, this is horrible'."

Inflation has also ticked up from 3% when Trump took office to 3.7% today, and economists estimate it would have been lower without his sweeping regime of global tariffs.

There is concern among Republicans that this economic picture has left them vulnerable in typically safe races, in states such as Texas, Ohio and Kansas.

"The southern states, the midwestern states, the American heartland - that is where Republicans tend to thrive," said Stephen Hawkins, the global director of research at the pollster More in Common.

"But that is where the Senate races that are so interesting are playing out right now."

"Places where President Trump won by 10, 12, 15 points just two years ago in the presidential race are now states where Democrats have a very viable chance of taking a Senate seat," he said.

When I asked voters in Iowa, a state Trump won in 2024 that has been hit by soaring fuel and fertiliser costs, whether the president would make people more or less likely to back Republicans - the answer was revealing.

"With the current climate, I would think possibly less, believe it or not," Paul Ross told me outside a busy college football game. "As a Republican myself, I would think it might be detrimental."

"I think it definitely puts voters off, there's no doubt about that, and I do think it probably raises the Democratic side to a level that isn't always there, just because it's Donald Trump," added Zach Shimp.

"He's got us in the war," another voter, Rose Heming, said. "Prices and groceries [are] high - sky high - gas is sky high."

That is the story of this election. Many voters, including in solidly Republican states, are hurting financially and polls suggest they may want to make this known at the ballot box on Tuesday.

But it is too simplistic to think this backdrop of war, tariffs and soaring prices will usher in a thumping Democratic victory in the House, Senate and governors' races.

Many Republican voters are angry with the president, but not so angry that they would vote for a Democrat. It is a mistake to assume that Trump's weak approval ratings translate to increasing popularity for the other side.

In fact, final polls taken before the elections suggest Trump's approval rating is around 38%. That is low - but the same polls, including a national NBC poll released on Sunday, indicate that only 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively.

Voter frustration is no guarantee of a willingness to switch sides on Tuesday.

"We like to stay out of people's business," Tim McKinnon, a Republican in Iowa who voted for Trump in 2024 told me last month. "And so [Trump's] world stage interventions time after time after time - we don't love it.

"We didn't expect him to necessarily be a perfect choir boy obviously," his wife, Michelle, added. "We voted for the underbelly of what he was standing for."

The Democratic Party cannot rely on voters like the McKinnons, who are frustrated with elements of Trump's recent agenda, to back them. They do not think Democrats will ever reflect their Christian, conservative values.

"One dollar more on gas is not going to change what we believe in," Tim McKinnon told me.

If Democrats do win a large swathe of seats on Tuesday night, it won't necessarily be because voters love them – they just hate them a little less.

The party, however, is already looking ahead to a 2028 presidential election in which they will have to unite behind a single candidate. That is easier said than done given their clear fractures - some of which spilled out publicly during this election cycle, including in Michigan over the weekend.

Democrats will be closely watching these results for lessons ahead of 2028. Can they really win in Texas? Can they tempt rural voters in deep Republican strongholds? And will some of their rising stars, such as Jon Ossoff in Georgia and James Talarico in Texas, live up to the hype?

If the answer to some of these questions is no, there will be much to ponder for the party over the next year. And the post-mortem may not be pretty.

"This represents an opportunity, really, for Democrats to expand a lot of their influence, not just in terms of numbers, but in terms of perception of where they can compete," Hawkins, from the pollster More in Common, said.

Republican attempts, including from Trump himself, to paint the Democrats as dangerous communists have not landed with all voters.

In Detroit, Michigan, Nicole Williams - who owns her own hairdressing salon - summed up the view of many people I spoke to. "Anything is better than what we have now," she said. "Socialist? Socialised? It don't matter to me. Lower my cost of living."

"People are just tired of the disrespect to Americans, because he is an American," Gwen Jackson, another Michigan voter, said, referring to the state's left-wing Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed who Trump has repeatedly attacked.

"People are just tired," she said. "They're ready to see a change."

Even when a sitting president is more popular than Trump, their party usually loses seats in the midterms. This, combined with the latest polling, means there is confidence among Democrats that they will at least win the House of Representatives.

"It's the cost of living, it's the undeclared war," Democratic strategist Mary Anne Marsh said of the key issues. "Every Republican who did not stand up to Donald Trump is about to realise the consequences of believing he was invincible."

If the Democrats do win the House, the party could try to block any legislation Trump wants to pass. That is unlikely to worry him, given he has already tried to bypass Congress as much as possible and rule by signing executive orders from the Oval Office instead.

Trump will be more concerned about the investigations Democrats will be able to launch if they take control of the House. They may also try to impeach some of his cabinet members, with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth seen as a likely candidate due to the war in Iran.

Winning the Senate on Tuesday is likely to be a much harder task for Democrats.

Thirty-five seats are up for election, and they will need a net gain of four to win control. If they lose in Michigan - a battleground seat they already hold - they will need a net gain of five seats to win it.

Most of the battleground races are close and several sit within the margin of error for pollsters. The crucial Senate races to watch are in Michigan, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Maine, Alaska and North Carolina.

This is, in reality, where these midterm elections will be won and lost.

There is, as always with American elections, an important caveat around the polls. They have historically overestimated the Democratic Party and underestimated President Trump, who appears convinced that he can once again defy them.

But if the polls are close to correct about the suggested surge of support for Democrats, then he could be looking at painful defeats in states that have been reliable Republican strongholds for decades.

How Trump may respond to any stinging losses is an open question. He has repeatedly questioned the integrity and security of these elections, and the possibility that he does so again as votes are still being counted or when results are declared is a very real one.

These elections, however, represent a hugely significant moment for Americans, many of whom want to see real change over the next two years.

For both parties, they will serve as the final electoral test before a 2028 presidential election that will determine what a post-Trump politics looks and feels like. And for the president himself, they are an opportunity for voters to cast judgement on how he and his party are performing.

As Trump looks to shape his legacy in the next two years, the question is whether a change in control of Congress, which he has largely bypassed, would really curb his presidency at all.

item.title: US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections
item.description: US officials described the attacks on Qeshm Island as limited and defensive, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.
item.content:encoded:
The US has launched strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.

The officials described the strikes as limited and said they were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing on a US aircraft.

Iranian state news agency Irna reported several explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment, but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 reconnaissance drones south of the island as well as a US MQ-9 drone over an area east of the Strait of Hormuz.

The BBC has contacted US Central Command (Centcom) for comment on the strikes, which came ahead of the US midterm elections.

Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.

Earlier on Monday, he told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran.

"One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," he told news outlet Axios. "They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it."

He also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme, in an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms.

This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump added.

There has been mounting speculation in the last few days that the US may resume significant strikes in Iran again after the midterms. But asked by a reporter on Monday if that was the case, Trump said "no".

Meanwhile, the Associated Press cited two regional officials as saying that, during a weekend phone call, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had pushed Trump for another wave of strikes on Iran following the midterms.

On Tuesday, Iran's chief negotiator with the US, parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, stated: "The ball is now in America's court to prevent war."

"Just as the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready for battle with its finger on the trigger, it has also given the American side a powerful and rational response," he said in a televised speech.

It was not immediately clear what Ghalibaf was referring to, but Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Irna on Monday that "very intensive" talks to try to end the war were under way with the US via Qatari and Pakistani mediators.

He also said Iran was prepared for both diplomatic and military scenarios "more than ever before" and that it was up to the US to choose between a "wise path" of negotiation or the "mistake of military aggression".

Last week, Iranian negotiators discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions. They reportedly include lifting a naval blockade of Iranian ports and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and the US naval blockade.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

item.title: Indonesia's toxic haze is giving its neighbours a political headache
item.description: Governments in Singapore and Malaysia are split between anxious citizens and an irascible neighbour.
item.content:encoded:
The haze billowing out from wildfires in the Indonesian regions of Kalimantan, Papua and Sumatra knows no borders.

Carried by winds to nearby Singapore and Malaysia, the toxic smog has in recent weeks impacted populations across maritime South East Asia, triggering respiratory illnesses and headaches.

It's also giving the region's governments a different kind of headache - split between the mounting frustrations of their citizens and the risk of souring diplomatic ties with Indonesia.

"People are fed up, angry and anxious," Eugene Tan, associate professor of law at the Singapore Management University, tells the BBC. "The governments have to respond to them, or else what is more an external issue has become an internal one with ample headroom for politicisation."

Indonesia's wildfires are a yearly occurrence, widely associated with industrial-scale land clearing to make way for crops like oil palm.

But the blazes this year have been particularly difficult to tame due to a strong El Niño, which has exacerbated drought conditions in the country's forests and peatlands.

Whereas previous haze episodes in Singapore and Malaysia have typically lasted for a few days, this time it stretched into weeks.

In Malaysia, locals started a boycott of Indonesian products in protest against the haze, after lawmaker Syed Saddiq called for sanctions on companies linked to the wildfires and said Malaysians should "treat them as an outcast in the region".

There have also been complaints in Singapore, a country that has come to expect seamless efficiency from its leaders.

"There appears to be the view that the government dropped the ball in dealing with the haze, given that it was known that the El Niño weather phenomenon would be severe and that early warning was given," says Tan.

"Clearly, Singaporeans expect the government to decisively deal with the polluters."

A diplomatic dilemma

Singapore's government, for its part, has made it clear that the haze problem is a priority.

Hundreds of haze shelters have been set up across the island, and masks are being distributed to children, the elderly and other vulnerable residents.

Authorities have also said they're looking to strengthen existing haze legislation and are investigating 10 Singapore-registered companies for potential links to the wildfires in Indonesia.

Last week, Singapore's foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan met Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto in Jakarta for what the former described as "honest" and "sincere" conversations that produced "constructive approaches".

The meeting came as both countries announced they would set up a joint task force to deal with the haze - an apparent détente after weeks of simmering bilateral tensions.

As the haze spiralled into yet another crisis for Prabowo's beleaguered administration, some officials pushed back against criticism.

One senior official ruffled feathers when he said the wildfires were out of human control and that oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".

That remark was "disappointing" and "not right", according to Singaporean senior minister K Shanmugam - a rare rebuke from the city state, which prides itself on its diplomatic prowess.

"The haze is affecting our health seriously, and it's really unacceptable," Shanmugam told reporters. Since the haze impacts citizens on both sides of the border, there should not be "any bilateral issues" in addressing it, he added.

"The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interest as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."

Days later, Indonesia announced it would reduce gas exports to Singapore, citing domestic energy needs - a move that many saw as retaliation to Singapore's rhetoric.

To be sure, Indonesia has faced recent electricity shortages in parts of the country. Singapore also says the reduction, which amounts to less than 2% of its total daily demand, will have little impact on its gas supply.

But the abrupt announcement came just days after Indonesia's energy minister warned that they could halt gas exports to countries that don't "respect Indonesia". That same day, Prabowo made reference to "countries that like to insult Indonesia" when talking about the wildfires.

"It's a tired playbook of using Singapore as the bogeyman, driven by the 'abang-adik' [big brother-little brother] syndrome," Tan says, referring to a historical dynamic that Singapore's leaders have long tried to shrug off: the expectation that it should defer to its larger neighbours.

"Singapore leaders expressing concerns about the haze and how it affects the people of both countries have been taken to mean that Singapore has been disrespectful to its neighbour."

Waiting for winds to change

In contrast, Malaysia's official rhetoric on the haze has been relatively muted.

Its foreign minister Mohamad Hasan has ruled out lodging a formal diplomatic protest with Indonesia or taking legal action, saying such actions "would mean we were prepared to sever relations".

For now, Malaysia has agreed to explore a memorandum of understanding with Indonesia to strengthen wildfire prevention efforts.

It would also rely on diplomatic mechanisms, Mohamad said - like the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.

The agreement, which came into effect in 2003, commits members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to collaborate on tackling the recurring haze.

But many see it as toothless, as it is unable to punish agricultural companies linked to wildfires or to force individual governments to do so.

The agreement has turned out to be "just not worth the paper it was signed on", says James Chin, professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.

"The moment the haze disappears, the moment the political pressure's off, it's back to business as usual."

In 2016, Asean countries had set a goal to eliminate haze in the region by 2020. When that deadline drifted quietly by, they set a new target of achieving the goal by 2030 instead.

Complicating Malaysia's position is the fact that it is also a major palm oil producer. The commodity is often linked to commercial "slash-and-burn" practices that are widely blamed for the region's wildfires.

Malaysia has at times dealt with acute haze stemming from blazes on local land.

In 2019, when Malaysia pointed to hotspots in Indonesia's peatlands as the cause of the haze shrouding the region, Indonesian authorities pointed the finger back at Malaysia, claiming the smog came from their side.

"As long as we place a lot of importance on oil palm planting, [the haze] is going to recur," says Ei Sun Oh, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia.

And even if Malaysia were to speak up, Oh adds, it's unlikely to wield the same "leverage" over Indonesia as Singapore, which is Indonesia's largest foreign investor and an offshore financial hub for many wealthy Indonesians.

For now, Malaysia "doesn't want to unduly provoke Indonesia", says Oh.

"The government is just wringing their hands till the wind blows [the problem] over. Because eventually it will blow over."

item.title: Apple unsure when more foldable iPhones will be available after selling out
item.description: Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo was a hit with people willing to spend $2,000 on a new mobile.
item.content:encoded:
The new head of Apple says the company is working to get its new foldable iPhones available to more people after the $1,999 smartphone quickly sold out when it was released just over a week ago.

John Ternus, who in September took over the role as Apple's chief executive from Tim Cook, said on Monday that he was "thrilled" at the early reaction to the iPhone Duo.

While the costly phone, which sells for £1,999 in the UK, immediately sold out, some buyers have seen their screens crack.

The phones are still in high demand and Sabhi Kahn, Apple's new chief operating officer, said the technology giant did not know when more Duos would be available.

"At this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance," Kahn said during a call with financial analysts to discuss Apple's latest financial results.

Apple executives did not mention during the call any issues with the iPhone Duo. But last week, the company said it would replace any phones that were impacted by an issue that caused a "small number" of the new phones to crack along the inside fold.

Nevertheless, Apple said on Monday that over the last year it sold more iPhones globally than it ever has before.

During the three months to 26 September, which did not include sales of the iPhone Duo that went on sale toward the end of October, Apple saw iPhone sales rise 17% to $57bn.

Apple has boasted throughout the year that iPhone sales have been surging, despite the company's warnings that crucial components for the device, along with Mac computers and iPads, were constrained to the point of weighing down sales.

Sales of Mac computers also grew during the quarter by 27%, hitting $10.7bn, another record for Apple.

Overall sales at the company rose by 15% for the year, to $479bn.

However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and Watch fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.

Kahn noted during the call that most Apple devices are still seeing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with "advanced nodes."

Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allows Apple's devices to operate more quickly, most of which Apple has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.

Khan said that such supply constraints are expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs. The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.

Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of Apple devices to store data like apps, photos, and text messages.

Much of that memory storage runs through data centres which have seen a huge boom in demand for space as artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots and platforms, including those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic, have become popular.

As demand for memory has grown, storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.

Cook had earlier this year referred to the sudden increase in data centre costs that Apple was seeing as a "thousand year flood."

It has led to the company raising prices on essentially all of its hardware products by around 20%.

item.title: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
item.description: The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by the US Treasury.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.

The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.

He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.

The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.

In Rwanda's case, Washington also raised concerns about human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights.

The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by US Treasury for its alleged role in the armed rebellion in eastern DR Congo.

The US Treasury said Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.

For South Africa, the US additionally pointed to corruption.

"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.

The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.

Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.

US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa.

"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.

item.title: Who are the victims of the deadly Florida jet crash?
item.description: Sunday's crash killed all nine people aboard, including a tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old copilot.
item.content:encoded:
Nine people have been killed after a small jet crashed and exploded in Florida on Sunday.

The Learjet 60 was bound for the Bahamas from Austin when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway.

The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating whether ice and turbulence contributed to the crash, and whether human error played a role.

Here is what we know so far about the victims.

Adam Robinson and Helen Sharp

The Texas tech entrepreneur, his wife Helen Sharp and their two children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, were all killed in the crash, according to a joint statement from some of the families of those killed.

Their family described them as "devoted parents" and said their children were "the light of their lives".

"Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever. Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives," the statement reads.

On his LinkedIn page, Robinson described himself as the founder and CEO of RB2B and Retention.com, and the CEO of Moltsets.

He previously worked at global financial services business Lehman Brothers and the banking group Barclays.

The BBC has contacted the companies for a statement.

Fellow tech entrepreneur Jesse Ouellette posted on LinkedIn about Robinson's death, saying he had helped him when he was building his company.

"He became a friend and someone I saw eye to eye with on how to build software companies," wrote Ouellette.

"He could disagree with you about almost anything, and somehow you'd walk away liking him even more."

Robinson's last post on the networking site was on Sunday, about a debate he and Ouellette had scheduled for the following week.

Helen Sharp, meanwhile, was an artist, according to media reports.

Her father, Dudley Sharp, told the Florida news site The Palm Beach Post that news his family had been on the plane was "quite a blow".

"We had a daughter, her husband and two grandchildren on the plane," he said.

Rachel Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina

Reed, Fehr and Cetina were also travelling aboard the jet with Robinson Sharp and their children.

Reed and Fehr were described in the joint family statement as "full of joy and adventure".

"They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation. From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building," it added.

It was not immediately clear what their relationship was with Robinson and Sharp.

The statement said Cetina "cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family".

It added: "She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion."

Jeff Gregory

Gregory, 55, has been identified as the pilot of the plane, according to East Coast Jets, a private charter company where Gregory used to work.

"We are deeply saddened to learn that Captain Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives in yesterday's tragic aviation accident in Palm Beach," a spokesperson for the company said in a statement on Monday.

Jeff worked for East Coast Jets "briefly" in 2016 and 2017, the spokesperson said.

Nathalia Filgueiras

US media has identified Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, as the copilot of the plane. She earned her pilot's licence when she was 17.

Filgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the fireball.

Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."

In a 2023 interview with a local news affiliate of CBS News, Filgueiras spoke proudly of receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school.

"I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes, but I can't drive a car, I mean I can but, a lot of people think it's funny."

item.title: A thousand job applications, five interviews and still no job
item.description: Annual Scottish figures on young people not in education, employment or training are due later - one young woman shares her struggle.
item.content:encoded:
Casey Smith has been going to the job centre every few weeks since she was 16 but feels she's been "going round and round in circles".

The teenager, from Johnstone, Renfrewshire, is one of nearly a million young people in the UK classified as a Neet - not in education, employment or training.

After four years, she is desperate to work.

"I'm nearly 20 now," she told BBC Scotland.

"I at least thought by the time I was 18, 17 that I would have something and I don't.

"I'm very frustrated about it because the amount of pressure that is on young adults nowadays is absolutely insane."

'Checking emails every day'

The Scottish government will release annual figures on young people's work status later.

Last year the figures revealed that 93% of those aged 16-19 were in education, employment or training.

Those who are between 20 and 24 are more likely to be Neet than those aged 16-19 in the UK.

Casey is just about to enter that cohort. She says she is "constantly" applying for jobs.

"I think I've definitely applied to a thousand, maybe just a wee bit under that.

"You're waking up every day and you're doing the same thing, applying and applying, and you're not hearing anything.

"I've had roughly five interviews," she said.

She explained that as soon as she wakes up she is checking emails and applying for all sorts of jobs including in cleaning, retail and hospitality.

Casey hands in CVs and has phoned every store in her local area twice looking for work.

"If I had it my way I would be doing a nine-to-five every day. I would love to do that."

The majority of Neets in the UK - 60% - are economically inactive, meaning they are not searching for work or able to start work.

Former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn is leading an official review into Neets and is expected to recommend major reforms designed to get many young people off benefits and into work in the coming weeks.

For Casey, the current system at the job centre just isn't working.

"I go once every two weeks and you're supposed to be there for roughly half an hour and have a conversation about what you can do.

"I will sit in the waiting area for maybe 20 minutes and then I will be speaking to whoever it is I'm speaking to for no more than five.

"And it's honestly it's like seeing somebody in the street that you've not seen in a wee while: 'Hi, how are you, what have you been up to? Ok, see you later'."

She says she is sometimes referred to community projects for assistance.

"They will teach you how to do things like making CVs or there might be a couple people looking for young people to start working for them", she said.

"However, it never gets anywhere.

"They're telling me to go out and do these things which I have already done several times over."

'More feedback'

Job hunting for years can take it's toll on confidence and mental health, she said.

"I think the pressure of it all is what really bugs me. Why is there so much pressure on me when you know that I try every single day yet I'm not getting anywhere with it?

"It's also embarrassing to talk about, because, I don't have anything, neither do my peers.

"And then when people who are older than us are like, 'Oh, have you got a job yet?'

"And it's just constant pressure, constant judgement."

Figures from Scotland last year revealed that 16-19 year olds from the poorest backgrounds were more than five times less likely to be participating in education, training or employment than those who lived in the least deprived areas.

Casey thinks there needs to be more feedback from employers when rejecting applicants and that those at the job centre could talk more about ideas for work, volunteering or experience.

"I know we have the job centre that's supposed to help us go out and get jobs and find work and things like that, but that's not working.

"That's falling to bits. I don't think it's going to be up and running in like the next 10 years.

"It's collapsing and nobody's doing anything about it.

"So once that crumbles and just does not work anymore, what do you expect us to do?

"We need a new system in place."

A spokesman for the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), which is responsible for Job Centres, said: "Every young person deserves the chance to build a future they are proud of.

"That is why we are investing £2.5bn to help more young people earn or learn, including through a Youth Hub in every local area, bringing together housing, mental health and employment support.

"And we are transforming Jobcentres to create a more personalised, modern and accessible service to support people across the country into work."

item.title: Democrat Stevens defends endorsement switch to Republican Rogers two days before election
item.description: But she refuses to be drawn on her rationale for switching candidates in the closely-fought US Senate race.
item.content:encoded:
A prominent Michigan Democrat who switched her endorsement to the Republican candidate in the final days of the vital Senate race has defended her decision, saying simply: "I changed my mind".

Haley Stevens, who unsuccessfully ran to become the Democratic nominee, withdrew support for the Democratic candidate who beat her in the primary contest, Abdul El-Sayed.

Ahead of the US midterm elections on Tuesday, Stevens gave her last-minute backing to Republican Mike Rogers, sparking widespread condemnation from her Democratic colleagues.

Stevens and El-Sayed have clashed on a range of issues, including US support for Israel. Michigan is considered critical for Democrats' hopes of winning control of Congress in the midterms.

Hours after the announcement, appearing on CNN, she said: "I woke up this morning clear-eyed, fresh and focused on what was in my heart, and that's that."

The seat is currently in Democratic hands. Analysts say the party needs to retain it, and win a handful of others from the Republicans, if it is to gain control of the US Senate and try to challenge US President Donald Trump in his final two years.

Stevens had previously offered her endorsement to El-Sayed after conceding defeat to him during a closely-fought primary contest in August.

As recently as Saturday night, she was said by CNN to be sticking with the fellow Democrat, and was denying any suggestion she would switch sides.

In her interview with the network the following day, Stevens did not provide her specific rationale, saying: "I changed my mind. (El-Sayed) said, 'Hey, I don't need your endorsement.' That's fine. Why the anger? Why the frustration?"

Stevens insisted that "nothing with me changed". She added that she was now "rock solid" in her choice to back Rogers, although insisted: "I still love my party a whole lot."

Fellow Democrats who condemned the Stevens endorsement were also critical of her interview performance. It was described as "painful" by Debbie Dingell, who, like Stevens, currently represents Michigan in the House of Representatives.

A public feud between Stevens, a centrist Democrat, and El-Sayed, who represents the party's left wing, has boiled over in recent days.

Stevens gave her endorsement to Rogers just two days before the election - making a surprise appearance alongside the Republican on Sunday.

"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted to X shortly afterwards. "Who we are as Michiganders is not hate," and then went on to say: "That's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers," Stevens said.

The move stunned many of her fellow party members, who condemned her decision to switch her support just two days before the election.

Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the US Senate, called it "despicable betrayal", and many of the Stevens staff reportedly resigned immediately after her announcement.

Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel wrote on X that Stevens is "not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future".

Republicans, meanwhile, applauded the move. Rogers himself said the move showed "courage", and Trump agreed that Stevens had been "very brave".

Stevens's schedule for Sunday initially involved her appearing at an event alongside El-Sayed, but she was reportedly asked by him not to come earlier in the weekend.

As Stevens instead made her appearance alongside Rogers, she said: "This is a very close election, we all know that, but Abdul made clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn't need me there, that he didn't want me there."

When asked about Stevens' endorsement, El-Sayed told reporters he was focused on the problems that were facing people in the state.

"At the end of the day, I don't think about Haley Stevens," he said on Sunday. "None of this matters."

Throughout the Michigan race, El-Sayed's strong criticism of Israel has been a source of tension within his party.

A recent flashpoint involved an advert that came from an outside liberal group. The advert linked rising prices in the US with American support for Israel. Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn it. El-Sayed said he did not agree with the advert's contents and said he had nothing to do with its contents, which was welcomed by Stevens.

The Michigan contest more broadly is one of the most closely-watched and bitter contests of the midterms.

El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim person ever elected to the US Senate, has faced a variety of attacks from Rogers and Trump.

The president has invoked 9/11 and called him a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.

item.title: Martha Stewart says she 'really screwed up' with homeless Halloween costume
item.description: The veteran lifestyle guru has deleted a photo of herself wearing torn clothes and dirt on her face.
item.content:encoded:
Veteran lifestyle guru Martha Stewart has admitted she "really screwed up" by dressing as a homeless person for Halloween.

The 85-year-old US entrepreneur and personality has deleted a photo of herself wearing torn clothes and dirt on her face, holding a sign saying: "I am hungry help me!!"

She posted a statement on Sunday saying she was "distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention".

That was followed by a fuller apology. "It's hard to admit when you've really screwed up. My earlier statement didn't go far enough. I know many people are suffering economically. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry."

Stewart had captioned her original Instagram photo: "My QVC candles are perfect for Halloween!!!"

The post received a swift and sharp backlash.

"This sartorial take on a homeless person is a lot. Insulting? Demeaning? Confusing? All of the above," PR expert Molly McPherson wrote.

One person wrote on social media: "Why in the hell would you even think about wearing that as a costume?"

Another said: "Why would she do that? Who did she think would find that funny? Billionaires?"

Arguably the original lifestyle influencer, Stewart started a catering business in the 1970s and rose to fame in the 1990s when she started her own magazine, Martha Stewart Living.

She later became a billionaire, albeit briefly, when her media empire Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia was floated on the stock market in 1999.

But in 2004 she was sentenced to five months in prison after she was found guilty on a number of charges related to an insider trading scandal.

She has since attempted to rebuild her brand, starring in her own reality television show, expanding her food products and teaming up with rapper and friend Snoop Dogg for a television series.

In 2015, she sold Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia for more than $350m (£220m).

item.title: Prosecutors hint at retrial for Lindsay Clancy on murder charges
item.description: Judge William Sullivan said if the case is headed to a retrial, that could happen as soon as March 2027.
item.content:encoded:
Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

Massachusetts prosecutors have given their clearest indication yet that they plan to retry Lindsay Clancy for the murder of her three children in 2023.

At a hearing on Monday, Judge William Sullivan scheduled a 16 November hearing where he plans to rule on a handful of motions that could determine how a retrial would proceed, including a request to dismiss the first-degree murder charges.

Clancy faced a weekslong trial on those charges over the summer. It fell apart in early September after a 12-person jury failed to reach a verdict.

If there is a retrial, Judge Sullivan said, it could happen as soon as March 2027.

The prosecution did not say on Monday whether Clancy would face the same charges or amended charges in the event of a retrial.

When the parties meet again later this month, they will hear the judge's rulings on the motions argued in court on Monday, and potentially will discuss dates for a retrial, Judge Sullivan said.

Kevin Reddington, Clancy's attorney, pushed the judge for a spring trial.

"I am not going to have this woman sit incarcerated for the next year or two or three," he said. "I want a date and I want it this spring."

But prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said she wants to hear Judge Sullivan's rulings on Monday's arguments before the prosecution commits to a new date or specifics for a potential retrial.

When the judge asked for more details on how prosecutors planned to proceed with a potential retrial, Sprague responded: "This would be a retrial - as to what that looks like will depend".

But that appeared to frustrate Reddington.

"Why do we not know if the next trial is going to be murder in the first degree or a lesser charge, why do they need to wait for the motions? I need to know logistically."

Clancy was charged with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.

Prosecutors could decide to bring lesser charges against Clancy in a retrial. For example, second-degree-murder charges, apply to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning.

Despite Sprague's statement in court, District Attorney Timothy Cruz has not yet confirmed that Clancy will face a retrial and has not announced future plans for the case.

Much of Monday's conversations in court focused on the one holdout juror, also known as Juror Doe, and the defence's investigation into him. Juror Doe disagreed with the other jurors, who appeared to want to find Clancy not guilty by way of insanity. The lack of agreement led to a hung jury and mistrial.

In some of the most fiery moments of the three-hour hearing on Monday, Reddington requested a plethora of evidence including the holdout juror's phone and phone records.

Heather O'Connor, the attorney who represents Juror Doe, said she was in court because Clancy's defence team has "combined several allegations" to try to argue that a mistrial should not have been declared, she said.

That is among the motions Sullivan said he will rule on in a few weeks.

Clancy does not deny killing her children, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors claim the killings were intentional.

item.title: King's role is not policy making, says Palace in slavery apology row
item.description: Buckingham Palace says the King has a unifying role in the Commonwealth rather than making political decisions.
item.content:encoded:
The King's role as head of the Commonwealth is about "inspiring and convening, rather than policy making", says Buckingham Palace - distancing him from rows over whether the UK should apologise and make reparations for its part in the Atlantic slave trade.

The Palace statement clarifying the King's non-political role in the Commonwealth comes as the organisation's leaders gather for a summit in Antigua and Barbuda.

The King is to deliver a speech on Tuesday which is expected to recognise the painful legacy of slavery. But his speech will reflect the position of the UK government.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had suggested there could be some form of apology over slavery, but has ruled out financial reparations.

The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.

On Saturday, the prime minister said that the UK "must face up to the past" over the "brutal and barbaric violation" of the slave trade, and that he was "open" to the possibility of a formal apology.

But on Monday, his official spokesperson said that while Burnham had "expressed his sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering caused by the transatlantic slave trade", this was "distinct from a formal apology".

Burnham thought it was "right that a formal apology is discussed properly with the countries and communities most affected", his spokesperson said.

"An apology of this significance should be informed by the people and countries most affected," they added.

Meanwhile Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK was "self-confident enough to have this conversation".

"The dialogue we're setting up will consider whether and how a formal apology could help acknowledge the history, help heal the division and support stronger relationships for the future," he said.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has rejected "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving the UK's current problems.

Gaston Brown, Prime Minister of Antigua and Barbuda, the country which is hosting the Commonwealth gathering, says that the consequences of slavery "have not disappeared with the passage of time" and wants to discuss reparations.

Whichever way the King's speech addresses the subject of slavery will be a political decision.

On previous occasions, the King has used strong language, such as talking about his "greatest sorrow and regret" at the "abhorrent and unjustifiable acts of violence" of the colonial era on a visit to Kenya.

And in Antigua he is expected to voice his "sincere sorrow", having spoken about the "great suffering of the past" in the Bahamas last week.

But any formal apology and any action on reparations on behalf of the UK would be a decision for political leaders - and the statement from the Palace defuses any expectation of such an intervention.

Instead the Palace sets out the King's role as a unifying figure above such divisions, with the Commonwealth described as a "family" of nations.

The King's "most significant contribution has been helping to connect leaders, institutions and investors - many of whom he knows personally from his many years of international diplomacy", says the Palace.

And that relates to "shared areas of interest and concern, creating the conditions in which ambitious Commonwealth-led initiatives can emerge and succeed".

It's a view of a positive and collective approach of the King's role in the Commonwealth, bringing together politicians with business leaders, philanthropists and civil society.

Sign up here to get the latest royal stories and analysis every week with our Royal Watch newsletter. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

item.title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
item.description: The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C.
item.content:encoded:
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.

Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.

Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.

Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".

He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.

Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.

"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.

The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).

It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.

In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.

Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.

In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce.

The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.

Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.

A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.

Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".

In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.

A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".

"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.

One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."

The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.

Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.

In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.

The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.

The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.

In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.

A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.

A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

Additional reporting by Shiona McCallum
